claim: β-arrestin-1 is an essential component in a signaling complex encompassing ADGRG2 and CFTR in the efferent ductules.
source: whereas CFTR was co-immunoprecipitated with ADGRG2 in WT and Arrb2-/- mice, it was not found in ADGRG2-immunoprecipitated complexes from the efferent ductules derived from Arrb1-/- mice, further suggesting that β-arrestin-1 is an essential component in a signaling complex encompassing ADGRG2 and CFTR in the efferent ductules (Figures 5H and 9L and Figure 9—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and inference

claim: Overexpression of β-arrestin-1 but not β-arrestin-2 promoted the interaction between ADGRG2 and CFTR in HEK293 cells.
source: Overexpression of β-arrestin-1 but not β-arrestin-2 promoted the interaction between ADGRG2 and CFTR (Figure 9—figure supplement 3), confirming the essential role of β-arrestin-1 in assembly of ADGRG2/CFTR coupling
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in HEK293 cells shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3

claim: The overexpression of ADGRG2 causes constitutive Gs and Gq coupling activity in vitro.
source: In vitro, the overexpression of ADGRG2 causes constitutive Gs and Gq coupling activity; a stronger effect is observed with ADGRG2β (Figure 10—figure supplements 2–5)
evidence: Supported by cAMP and NFAT-DLR assay data shown in Figure 10—figure supplements 2–5

claim: A stronger constitutive activity effect is observed with ADGRG2β compared to ADGRG2FL.
source: In vitro, the overexpression of ADGRG2 causes constitutive Gs and Gq coupling activity; a stronger effect is observed with ADGRG2β (Figure 10—figure supplements 2–5)
evidence: Supported by cAMP and NFAT-DLR assay data shown in Figure 10—figure supplements 2–5

claim: The co-expression of ADGRG2 and CFTR significantly increased the amplitude and slope of the current responses.
source: The co-expression of ADGRG2 and CFTR significantly increased the amplitude and slope of the current responses, which were significantly reduced by the CFTR inhibitor CFTRinh-172, compared with cells transfected with CFTR alone, indicating that CFTR channels are activated by ADGRG2 in a recombinant system (Figure 10B–D)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 10B–D

claim: CFTR channels are activated by ADGRG2 in a recombinant system.
source: The co-expression of ADGRG2 and CFTR significantly increased the amplitude and slope of the current responses, which were significantly reduced by the CFTR inhibitor CFTRinh-172, compared with cells transfected with CFTR alone, indicating that CFTR channels are activated by ADGRG2 in a recombinant system (Figure 10B–D)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data and inference

claim: The application of FSK and IBMX further increased the whole-cell Cl- current in the presence of both ADGRG2 and CFTR.
source: the application of FSK and IBMX further increased the whole-cell Cl- current in the presence of both ADGRG2 and CFTR, confirming that ADGRG2 increased the basal activity of CFTR but did not stimulate CFTR to a full activation state (Figure 10B–C and Figure 10—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 10B–C and Figure 10—figure supplement 5A

claim: ADGRG2 increased the basal activity of CFTR but did not stimulate CFTR to a full activation state.
source: the application of FSK and IBMX further increased the whole-cell Cl- current in the presence of both ADGRG2 and CFTR, confirming that ADGRG2 increased the basal activity of CFTR but did not stimulate CFTR to a full activation state (Figure 10B–C and Figure 10—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data and inference

claim: Increased CFTR activity induced by ADGRG2 was significantly diminished by the PKC inhibitor Ro 31-8220.
source: Importantly, increased CFTR activity induced by ADGRG2 was significantly diminished by the PKC inhibitor Ro 31-8220 (Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 5B–D)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 5B–D

claim: ADGRG2 increases CFTR Cl- currents through the activation of Gq-PLC-PKC signaling.
source: these data demonstrate that ADGRG2 increases CFTR Cl- currents through the activation of Gq-PLC-PKC signaling
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data and pharmacological interventions

claim: A double mutation in the 'DRY' motif H696A/M697A of ADGRG2 eliminated coupling activity with both Gs and Gq.
source: Under the equal expression of these mutants in the cell membrane, a double mutation in the 'DRY' motif H696A/M697A of ADGRG2 eliminated coupling activity with both Gs and Gq (Figure 11B–C and Figure 11—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by cAMP and NFAT-DLR assay data shown in Figure 11B–C and Figure 11—figure supplement 2

claim: Y698A and F705A mutations significantly impaired the Gs coupling activity of ADGRG2 but did not exert significant effects on NFAT-DLR activity.
source: Three mutations in intracellular loop 2, specifically Y698A and F705A, significantly impaired the Gs coupling activity of ADGRG2 but did not exert significant effects on NFAT-DLR activity (Figure 11B–C)
evidence: Supported by cAMP and NFAT-DLR assay data shown in Figure 11B–C

claim: Y708A and R803E/K804E mutations nearly abolished the Gq coupling activity of ADGRG2 but did not have significant effects on intracellular cAMP levels.
source: However, Y708A in intracellular loop 2 and R803E/K804E in intracellular loop 3 nearly abolished the Gq coupling activity of ADGRG2 but did not have significant effects on intracellular cAMP levels compared with the WT ADGRG2
evidence: Supported by cAMP and NFAT-DLR assay data

claim: The Gq-dysfunctional mutant and the H696A/M697A double Gs/Gq signaling-defective mutant did not demonstrate coupling between ADGRG2 and CFTR.
source: Interestingly, although the mutant with a specific Gs signaling defect showed decreased coupling of ADGRG2 to CFTR, the Gq-dysfunctional mutant and the H696A/M697A double Gs/Gq signaling-defective mutant did not demonstrate coupling between ADGRG2 and CFTR (Figure 11D–F)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 11D–F

claim: Specific residues in intracellular loops 2 and 3 are determinants of the G protein subtype coupling of ADGRG2.
source: these results demonstrate that specific residues in intracellular loops 2 and 3 are determinants of the G protein subtype coupling of ADGRG2
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis and functional assay data

claim: Gq signaling is essential for CFTR activation in recombinant in vitro systems downstream of ADGRG2.
source: Furthermore, downstream of ADGRG2, Gq signaling is essential for CFTR activation in recombinant in vitro systems
evidence: Supported by whole-cell recording data with ADGRG2 mutants

claim: Conditional expression of WT ADGRG2 in the efferent ductules significantly reduced obstruction in Adgrg2-/Y mice.
source: The conditional expression of ADGRG2 in non-ciliated cells in Adgrg2-/Y mice significantly reduced this obstruction, whereas the expression of G protein signaling-deficient mutants of ADGRG2, including Y698A, F705A, Y708A, RK803EE and HM696AA, significantly reduced this rescue effect (Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Expression of G protein signaling-deficient mutants of ADGRG2 significantly reduced the rescue effect on obstruction in Adgrg2-/Y mice.
source: The conditional expression of ADGRG2 in non-ciliated cells in Adgrg2-/Y mice significantly reduced this obstruction, whereas the expression of G protein signaling-deficient mutants of ADGRG2, including Y698A, F705A, Y708A, RK803EE and HM696AA, significantly reduced this rescue effect (Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Conditional infection of the Gs/Gq double signaling-deficient mutant ADGRG2-HM696AA did not result in differing levels of accumulation in the efferent ductules compared with those in Adgrg2-/Y mice infected with a control virus.
source: Specifically, conditional infection of the Gs/Gq double signaling-deficient mutant ADGRG2-HM696AA or the Gq signaling-deficient mutants Y708A and RK803EE did not result in differing levels of accumulation in the efferent ductules compared with those in Adgrg2-/Y mice infected with a control virus
evidence: Supported by histological data

claim: The Gs signaling-deficient mutants Y698A and F705A exhibited improved rescue activity compared with the Gq mutants.
source: The Gs signaling-deficient mutants Y698A and F705A exhibited improved rescue activity compared with the Gq mutants (Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 12B–E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Exogenous introduction of WT ADGRG2 to non-ciliated cells nearly restored the appearance of sperm in the initial segment.
source: The exogenous introduction of WT ADGRG2 to non-ciliated cells nearly restored the appearance of sperm in the initial segment and significantly increased sperm numbers in the caput (Figure 12B and E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 12B and E and Figure 12—figure supplement 1C

claim: Conditional expression of the Gs-deficient mutations Y698A and F705A marginally reduced the inflation of the efferent ductules of Adgrg2-/Y mice.
source: conditional expression of the Gs-deficient mutations Y698A and F705A marginally reduced the inflation of the efferent ductules of Adgrg2-/Y mice, whereas the Gq signaling mutants did not exert significant effects on the luminal volume (Figure 13A–F)
evidence: Supported by ligation experiment data shown in Figure 13A–F

claim: The Gq signaling mutants did not exert significant effects on the luminal volume of efferent ductules.
source: conditional expression of the Gs-deficient mutations Y698A and F705A marginally reduced the inflation of the efferent ductules of Adgrg2-/Y mice, whereas the Gq signaling mutants did not exert significant effects on the luminal volume (Figure 13A–F)
evidence: Supported by ligation experiment data shown in Figure 13A–F

claim: There is a direct correlation between efferent ductule reabsorption ability and mature sperm numbers.
source: This result is consistent with the effects of these mutants on sperm numbers in the caudal epididymis, thereby suggesting a direct correlation between efferent ductule reabsorption ability and mature sperm numbers (Figures 12C and 13A–F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference

claim: Gq activity is required downstream of ADGRG2 for fluid reabsorption in the efferent ductules and sperm transportation.
source: our results demonstrate that Gq activity is required downstream of ADGRG2, and Gs function contributes to fluid reabsorption in the efferent ductules and sperm transportation
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with ADGRG2 mutants

claim: Gs function contributes to fluid reabsorption in the efferent ductules and sperm transportation.
source: our results demonstrate that Gq activity is required downstream of ADGRG2, and Gs function contributes to fluid reabsorption in the efferent ductules and sperm transportation
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with ADGRG2 mutants
